title: Can We Have a Fun Lesson Today?
author: Begum, Thahmina
source: TB Blogs, CST T&L Bulletin (tbeeblogs.wordpress.com), July 10, 2023
summary: Thahmina Begum tackles the end-of-term pressure to abandon planned teaching in favour of "fun" activities, arguing that because no two students agree on what counts as fun, chasing it is a losing game, while a school's codified approach to good teaching is something staff can actually agree on and rely on. She works through specific temptations teachers face under this pressure, showing an "educational" film, running an elaborate quiz-show review lesson, and argues each trades disproportionate planning time and lost curriculum time for questionable payoff, framing consistent, planned curriculum delivery as the better bet for students' actual life chances. She draws an extended analogy to endurance athletes, citing fatigue researcher Samuele Marcora's finding that the brain limits physical performance before the body's true physiological maximum is reached, and a study showing wall-sit endurance depended more on willpower than muscle fatigue, to argue that teachers' own capacity to keep teaching well to the end of a lesson or term is more mental than physical. She closes by refusing the fun-versus-learning dichotomy outright, arguing that if teachers front-load clear expectations and stay upbeat, well-executed planned teaching can be enjoyable in its own right without abandoning the curriculum.
points: Begum's core reframe treats "fun" as an unproductive target precisely because it's undefinable by consensus, redirecting energy toward good teaching, which is definable and something a school can actually codify and rely on.

She names two specific end-of-term temptations, an "educational" film and an elaborate quiz-show lesson, and argues both fail a simple cost-benefit test against their planning time and lost curriculum time.

Her Marcora and wall-sit research detour reframes teacher fatigue at the end of a demanding term as substantially a mental, motivational phenomenon rather than a purely physical one, implying it can be managed rather than simply endured.

Her closing line, "learning is not the antithesis of fun," explicitly rejects the binary the whole piece has been responding to, rather than conceding that planned teaching is simply the less-fun but more responsible choice.
quotes: No one can agree on what is ‘fun’. Luckily, there is something we do agree on (for now): what makes good teaching.
The time it took me to plan it all was equivalent to 5 lessons worth of planning.

Fatigue researcher, Dr Samuele Marcora says, ‘top-level athletes get closer and closer to their real physiological maximum’. But they never quite reach it; the brain applies the brakes before the heart, lungs and muscles fail.

The researchers found that the more money offered, the longer the subjects lasted – which makes sense – but the study illustrated something else: the timing of their collapse depended not on their muscles but on their willpower.
Learning is not the antithesis of fun. So let’s not treat it like it is. When we say ‘no’ to a film, don’t be apologetic about it.
